concepts.name: Scale and Frequency of Mongol Invasions under Alauddin Khilji
key_dimensions: Number and chronology of major invasions (1297–1308): Zafar Khan episode, Kili battle, Amroha, Ravi
Distinction between raids for plunder vs. attempts at permanent conquest
Why Alauddin faced more invasions than predecessors — geographic and political context
UPSC trap: conflating defensive victories with offensive campaigns against Mongols

concepts.name: Battle of Kili (1299) — Significance and Command Structure
key_dimensions: Role of Zafar Khan's insubordination and its consequences — disobedience vs. heroism debate
Alauddin's strategic restraint vs. Zafar Khan's aggressive charge: command discipline lesson
Outcome: Mongol withdrawal despite Zafar Khan's death — pyrrhic heroism
UPSC trap: confusing Kili with other battles like Amroha or Ravi in terms of commanders

concepts.name: Battle of Amroha (1305) — Malik Kafur and Mongol Defeat
key_dimensions: Role of Malik Nayak (Malik Kafur's early career association) and Ghazi Malik in command
Scale of Mongol defeat — largest Mongol force repulsed under Alauddin
Significance of capturing and executing thousands of Mongol prisoners
UPSC trap: attributing Amroha solely to Malik Kafur — actual commander was Malik Nayak/Ghazi Malik

concepts.name: Battle of Ravi (1306) — Ghazi Malik's Role and Long-term Implications
key_dimensions: Ghazi Malik (future Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) as the key general — continuity into Tughlaq era
Crossing into Mongol territory — first offensive pursuit by Delhi Sultanate
How Ravi victory laid groundwork for Ghazi Malik's political rise
UPSC trap: not recognizing Ravi as a turning point that effectively ended large-scale Mongol invasions

concepts.name: Alauddin Khilji's Military Reforms as Anti-Mongol Strategy
key_dimensions: Permanent standing army (paid in cash) vs. earlier iqta-based feudal levies — Diwan-i-Arz reforms
Introduction of dagh (branding of horses) and chehra (descriptive rolls) to prevent fraud
Standardization of salaries and reduction of prices to sustain large army affordably
UPSC trap: treating market reforms as purely economic — their primary motivation was military/anti-Mongol

concepts.name: Alauddin's Market Control Reforms (Chahalgani-era economics) as Mongol Defense Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Four markets of Delhi: grain, cloth, cattle/horses, general commodities — linkage to army provisioning
Price control mechanism: Shahna, Barids, Munhiyans — multi-layered surveillance
How artificially low prices allowed payment of lower salaries while maintaining soldier welfare
UPSC trap: treating market reforms and military reforms as separate — they formed one integrated anti-Mongol system

concepts.name: Fortification and Garrison Strategy under Alauddin Khilji
key_dimensions: Strengthening of Siri fort as a new capital — strategic choice over old Delhi
Forward garrison posts along northwestern passes (Sindh-Punjab corridor)
Role of Dipalpur and Multan as frontier buffer zones
UPSC trap: Siri is often listed only as architectural achievement — its primary purpose was military-defensive

concepts.name: The 'New Muslims' Problem — Mongol Converts and Internal Security
key_dimensions: Mongol prisoners converted to Islam settled in Delhi — 'New Muslims' (Nau Musalman)
Their role in the conspiracy of 1299 and Alauddin's brutal crackdown
Policy dilemma: Islamic obligation to protect converts vs. security threat they posed
UPSC trap: New Muslims episode is often overlooked but reveals the internal dimension of Mongol threat

concepts.name: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's (Ghazi Malik) Anti-Mongol Credentials and Rise to Power
key_dimensions: 29 engagements against Mongols as governor of Punjab — claimed by Barani
How anti-Mongol military success legitimized his seizure of the throne in 1320
Transition: from Alauddin's general to founder of Tughlaq dynasty — military merit vs. dynastic legitimacy
UPSC trap: underestimating how Mongol defense shaped Tughlaq dynasty's founding narrative

concepts.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Shift from Defense to Diplomacy with Mongols
key_dimensions: Relative absence of major Mongol invasions during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign
Diplomatic exchanges with Chagatai Khanate — shift from military to political containment
Whether the Khorasan and Iraq expedition plans were offensive responses to Mongol presence
UPSC trap: assuming Tughlaq period was free of Mongol concern — the threat shaped his ambitious but failed campaigns

concepts.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's Era — Decline of Mongol Threat and Its Political Consequences
key_dimensions: Mongol threat diminishes post-1330s due to internal fragmentation of Chagatai Khanate
Firuz's demilitarization: reduction of standing army, revival of iqta — possible because Mongol threat receded
Long-term consequence: military weakness that contributed to vulnerability before Timur's invasion (1398)
UPSC trap: Timur is not a 'Mongol' invasion per se — Timur was Turco-Mongol/Timurid, not Chagatai Mongol

concepts.name: Timur's Invasion (1398) — Distinction from Mongol Invasions and Tughlaq Collapse
key_dimensions: Timur as Timurid/Turco-Mongol — distinct from Chagatai Mongols who attacked Alauddin
Mahmud Tughlaq's flight and the effective end of Tughlaq authority
Timur's stated justification: punishing Delhi sultans for tolerating Hindus — religious vs. political motivation
UPSC trap: calling Timur's invasion a 'Mongol invasion' — technically and historically incorrect

concepts.name: Role of Punjab and Sindh as the Mongol Invasion Corridor
key_dimensions: Geographic inevitability: Khyber and Bolan passes as entry points — why northwest was perpetual vulnerability
Administrative importance of Punjab governorship — always given to trusted/capable commanders
How control of Punjab defined political legitimacy within the Sultanate
UPSC trap: overlooking that most battles (Kili, Amroha, Ravi) were fought in Punjab plain, not at passes

concepts.name: Mongol Invasions under Balban's Predecessors vs. Khilji Period — Comparative Context
key_dimensions: Earlier raids under Iltutmish and Balban: tribute payment and diplomatic appeasement vs. Alauddin's outright military defeat
Balban's 'blood and iron' policy — creating buffer in Punjab but not decisive military confrontation
Why Alauddin could go further: larger revenue base, professional army, centralized administration
UPSC trap: attributing anti-Mongol success solely to Alauddin without recognizing Balban's foundational work

concepts.name: Intelligence and Surveillance Systems (Barids and Munhiyans) in Mongol Defense
key_dimensions: Dual intelligence network: official Barids (state reporters) and secret Munhiyans (spies)
Their dual role: monitoring market prices AND frontier movements/internal conspiracies
How intelligence failures contributed to early Mongol successes (e.g., surprise raids)
UPSC trap: Barids and Munhiyans are taught only under administrative history — their military-intelligence function is underemphasized

concepts.name: Economic Burden of Perpetual Mongol Defense and Its Administrative Consequences
key_dimensions: Revenue extraction from Doab and Gujarat conquests to fund anti-Mongol army
Peasant oppression as a byproduct — contradiction between military efficiency and agrarian stability
Alauddin's admission (per Barani) that governance was improvised, not theoretically grounded
UPSC trap: treating Alauddin's harsh taxation as purely despotic — it was structurally necessitated by military expenditure

concepts.name: Mongol Convert Soldiers in the Delhi Sultanate Army — Integration and Risk
key_dimensions: Policy of absorbing defeated/surrendered Mongol warriors into the Sultanate army
Their military value vs. loyalty risk — the 1299 conspiracy as case study
Alauddin's post-conspiracy policy: mass killing of New Muslims — legality and precedent under Islamic law
UPSC trap: this concept bridges military history, religious policy, and administrative history — often set as analytical questions

concepts.name: Symbolic and Ideological Dimensions of Mongol Resistance — Legitimacy of Khilji and Tughlaq Rule
key_dimensions: Defending Dar-ul-Islam (abode of Islam) against pagan Mongols — religious legitimacy of sultans
How military victories against Mongols were used in court chronicles (Barani, Amir Khusrau) for political glorification
Amir Khusrau's 'Khaza'in-ul-Futuh' and 'Miftah-ul-Futuh' as propaganda documents on Mongol victories
UPSC trap: taking Barani and Khusrau's accounts of Mongol numbers at face value — both exaggerated for literary/political effect

concepts.name: Comparison of Alauddin Khilji and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq as Anti-Mongol Strategists
key_dimensions: Alauddin: centralized command, direct control, economic-military integration
Ghazi Malik: frontier governance model — decentralized but experienced provincial defense
Why Ghazi Malik's model was more sustainable but less transformative than Alauddin's
UPSC trap: treating them as similar — their approaches represent two distinct models of frontier defense that UPSC can test comparatively
